We call it attention-deficit disorder. Gabor Maté thinks that name hides more than it tells us (Maté, 1999). In *Scattered Minds* he makes a different case, and I find it hard to shake. The distractibility isn't a broken part — it's an adaptation. A nervous system learned, early and under stress, to tune out what it couldn't bear to tune in [1]. Why does that matter? Because it stops asking what's wrong with the kid. It starts asking what happened around the kid.

## The Biology of Attention

So where does he plant this? In the prefrontal cortex — the part of the brain that runs attention and impulse, and that mostly grows after birth [2]. Those circuits get wired by how attuned the caregivers are. Chronic stress in that early world can stunt them (Schore, 1994). So the kid a teacher reads as defiant, or lazy? That's a regulatory system showing us it never got what it needed.

I want to be careful here, because Maté is. He isn't saying parents cause it. Heredity hands you a sensitivity; the environment decides how it shows up [3]. That distinction matters. It takes away blame without taking away responsibility.

## What Follows From This

If it's an adaptation, medication can help — but it can't be enough. The real work is building, as adults, the relational conditions we missed as kids: patience, acceptance, the felt sense of being attuned to [4]. Maté calls it self-parenting. He's blunt that it's slow. Years, not weeks.

None of this makes the problem smaller. It makes it more human. And it points toward help that treats a whole person, not a set of symptoms to manage.
